title: Work ships before CI has run
body:
## What goes wrong
Work merges into the main branch without continuous integration ever running on it, and that goes unnoticed at merge time.

## Why it matters
Once CI silently stops gating merges, failing tests and type errors pile up on the main branch. New failures get waved off by eye as "flakes" instead of being run and checked, so real regressions blend in with noise.

## Evidence
Signal: `pr` (the share of merged changes where CI did not pass, via `count`).
At seeding: the one build this came from carried main-branch test and type failures that were never run to a clean result, with new failures compared by hand instead of re-run. Fixed when `merged_without_passing_ci` stays at zero for a normal week.

## Where the fix belongs
In the step that decides a change is ready to merge, and in how CI's own result gets read back before that decision.

Seen: 0 times since seeding

title: Security issues ship without being caught
body:
## What goes wrong
Issues with real security impact -- too much access granted, or data exposed to users who shouldn't see it -- reach production without a review stopping them.

## Why it matters
A security gap that ships is a security gap a user can hit; knowing about it after the fact is not a mitigation.

## Evidence
No signal in the current measurement set tracks this directly. At seeding: at least one such issue was already known, written up as a note, and merged anyway rather than fixed first. Fixed when a security pass runs before merge and nothing with this shape reaches the main branch again.

## Where the fix belongs
In the review step that runs before a change merges, and in what counts as "resolved" for a known risk.

Seen: 0 times since seeding

title: Parallel work lands without being reconciled
body:
## What goes wrong
When more than one lane of work touches the same area at once, nothing checks that the pieces agree with each other before they all land.

## Why it matters
Lanes that disagree on the same rules leave behind contradictions, duplicated logic and leftover scaffolding nobody owns, which costs more to untangle later than it would have cost to reconcile up front.

## Evidence
No signal in the current measurement set tracks this directly. At seeding: parallel lanes left duplicated helper logic, unused scaffolding and clashing change ordering behind. Fixed when an integration pass runs before parallel lanes merge, and this kind of contradiction stops showing up in review.

## Where the fix belongs
In how parallel lanes get merged together, with an integration step between "each lane is done" and "the whole thing is done."

Seen: 0 times since seeding

title: Tests pass without being able to fail
body:
## What goes wrong
Some tests are built so they can't catch a real regression: they skip when a dependency isn't present and still report success, they're written by whoever wrote the code they check, or they only exercise a stand-in instead of the real thing.

## Why it matters
A green suite that can't go red isn't evidence of anything. It gives false confidence at exactly the moment a real check was needed.

## Evidence
No signal in the current measurement set tracks this directly. At seeding: suites that short-circuit to a pass with no backing service present, tests written in the same change as the code they check, and one large suite built entirely against a stand-in instead of the real dependency. Fixed when a review step can show a given test actually fails on a broken version of the code it covers.

## Where the fix belongs
In what a review checks about a test's own ability to fail, before the test is trusted.

Seen: 0 times since seeding

title: Large changes merge within minutes of opening
body:
## What goes wrong
Sizeable changes open and merge almost immediately, reviewed only by other instances of the same model in the same sitting.

## Why it matters
A change nobody independent looked at, merged before anyone could, is not reviewed -- it just has a review-shaped step attached to it.

## Evidence
Signal: `pr` (`median_lines`, `median_open_to_merge_s`, via `count`). At seeding: changes of one to six thousand lines were merging within about a minute of opening. Fixed when the time from open to merge leaves room for an independent pass, as shown by `median_open_to_merge_s`.

## Where the fix belongs
In the step between opening a change and merging it -- what has to happen in between, and who has to do it.

Seen: 0 times since seeding

title: Commit messages claim fixes that aren't in the code
body:
## What goes wrong
A commit message says something was fixed or verified when the code in that commit doesn't actually do it. Departures from the agreed design get written up as "assumptions" rather than flagged for a decision.

## Why it matters
A message that overstates what a change does is worse than no message: it tells the next reader to stop looking right where they should look closer.

## Evidence
No signal in the current measurement set tracks this directly. At seeding: commit messages asserting fixes or verification not borne out by the diff, and spec departures logged as assumptions instead of raised. Fixed when a review step stops finding a claim in a commit message that the diff doesn't back up.

## Where the fix belongs
In what a commit message is allowed to claim, and in a review step that checks the message against the diff.

Seen: 0 times since seeding

title: Nearly every commit carries the same authorship trailer
body:
## What goes wrong
Commits are stamped with an attribution trailer naming the tool that wrote them, on almost every commit, regardless of what's wanted for that repository.

## Why it matters
An attribution line that's always there isn't a meaningful signal, and it's not something every repository wants in its history.

## Evidence
Signal: `pr` (`coauthor_trailers`, via `count`). At seeding: the trailer appeared on about 99 out of every 100 commits. Fixed when the trailer reflects a repository's own setting rather than always being present.

## Where the fix belongs
In the setting that controls whether this trailer gets added, made to follow what each repository actually wants.

Seen: 0 times since seeding

title: A long conversation's context never gets reset
body:
## What goes wrong
Context inside one long-running conversation keeps growing and is never reset, even once a piece of work inside it is done and its detail is no longer needed.

## Why it matters
Every turn after that pays, in time and cost, for carrying the entire history forward -- including turns that only needed to answer a small question.

## Evidence
Signal: `context_first`, `context_peak` (via `count`). At seeding: one session grew from about 24 thousand tokens to nearly 800 thousand over its life, and a sizeable share of turns started already above 100 thousand tokens for small asks. Fixed when `context_first` for ordinary turns stays well under that starting-size threshold.

## Where the fix belongs
In how a long-running conversation is built as its own project, with a deliberate point where old detail gets dropped rather than carried forever.

Seen: 0 times since seeding

title: Background work dies the moment its turn ends
body:
## What goes wrong
Work started in the background -- a subagent, a shell command left running -- lives only as long as the turn that started it. When the turn ends, that work is gone, whether or not it finished.

## Why it matters
Parallel work that can vanish mid-flight either has to be babysat by keeping the turn open, or it silently disappears and has to be redone.

## Evidence
Signal: `lost_background` (via `count`). At seeding: parallel work was lost this way more than once in a single day. Fixed when `lost_background` stays at zero across normal runs.

## Where the fix belongs
In how background work is run as its own project, so it outlives the turn that started it instead of depending on it staying open.

Seen: 0 times since seeding

title: Work rarely gets delegated
body:
## What goes wrong
Most turns do their own work directly in the main thread rather than handing pieces of it to a subagent, even on turns heavy enough with tool calls that delegating would help.

## Why it matters
Working everything in one thread means one context carries everything at once, and nothing runs in parallel or gets a fresh, focused context of its own.

## Evidence
Signal: `no_delegation` (via `count`). At seeding: only a small single-digit percentage of turns used any subagent at all, and well under half of the heaviest-tool-call turns used one. Fixed when `no_delegation`'s `turns` count stays near zero.

## Where the fix belongs
In what prompts a turn to delegate, and in making a maintained delegation workflow the default rather than something that has to be reached for.

Seen: 0 times since seeding

title: Code gets written through shell here-documents
body:
## What goes wrong
Instead of using a dedicated file-editing tool, code gets written by piping whole files through shell commands, with full file contents passed through the main context either way.

## Why it matters
Shell here-documents are a clumsy way to write code: they're easy to get wrong on quoting and escaping, and they put the entire file's text in context rather than just the lines that changed.

## Evidence
Signal: `inline_code_chars` (via `count`). At seeding: the large majority of main-thread tool calls were shell commands, and a dedicated edit tool was used only a couple of times across hundreds of turns. Fixed when `inline_code_chars` stays low and shell-based file writes stop being the default way code gets changed.

## Where the fix belongs
In which tool gets reached for by default when writing or changing a file.

Seen: 0 times since seeding

title: Project setup gets rediscovered every conversation
body:
## What goes wrong
Each new conversation on a project re-clones it and re-learns its setup from scratch, instead of picking up what an earlier conversation already worked out.

## Why it matters
Re-learning the same setup over and over burns time and disk space, and setup knowledge ends up scattered across several places instead of living in one.

## Evidence
Signal: `reclone` (via `count`). At seeding: a single project was cloned dozens of times over a few days, and the scratch space used ran into the tens of gigabytes. Fixed when `reclone`'s `turns` count stays near zero for a project already seen before.

## Where the fix belongs
In how a project's own setup and facts are found and reused across conversations, instead of being split across several sources and rebuilt each time.

Seen: 0 times since seeding

title: The fixed cost of starting a session keeps climbing
body:
## What goes wrong
Every fresh session pays a fixed token cost before any real work happens, and that baseline cost has been rising over time rather than staying flat.

## Why it matters
A rising fixed cost makes every single turn more expensive, even ones that do nothing unusual -- it's a tax that grows quietly in the background.

## Evidence
No signal in the current measurement set tracks this directly; it would show up as a slow upward drift in `context_first` across ordinary turns over days, not within one turn. At seeding: a fresh session's starting overhead rose by several thousand tokens over the course of a few days. Fixed when that baseline stops climbing and holds steady between changes.

## Where the fix belongs
In what gets loaded into every fresh session by default, and in keeping that content deliberately small.

Seen: 0 times since seeding

title: Background lanes aren't logged in, and new projects get turned away
body:
## What goes wrong
Lanes started in the background can fail all at once because the account running them isn't signed in, and a project the system hasn't already registered gets refused outright instead of being picked up.

## Why it matters
Either failure mode cuts a long run short for a reason that has nothing to do with the work itself, and both are avoidable setup problems rather than real obstacles.

## Evidence
No signal in the current measurement set tracks this directly. At seeding: several background lanes failed at once for not being signed in, and unregistered projects were refused rather than picked up automatically. Fixed when background lanes stay signed in on their own, and a new project doesn't need to be registered by hand before it's picked up.

## Where the fix belongs
In how a background lane's own login is kept current, and in how a new project gets registered.

Seen: 0 times since seeding

title: Long runs spend their own time budget waiting in place
body:
## What goes wrong
To keep a turn alive while something else finishes, the main thread sits in a loop that just waits, burning its own time budget on nothing.

## Why it matters
Time spent waiting in the foreground is time that isn't available for the turn's real budget, and it's a workaround for a gap rather than a way of actually tracking background work.

## Evidence
No signal in the current measurement set tracks this directly. At seeding: dozens of these waiting loops together ate several hours of the available turn budget in a few days of work. Fixed when a turn can wait on background work finishing without needing to sit in a loop to do it.

## Where the fix belongs
In how a turn is notified that background work finished, instead of polling for it by waiting in place.

Seen: 0 times since seeding

title: It goes quiet after promising a report
body:
## What goes wrong
A turn says it will report back once something finishes, and then the turn simply ends without ever following up. Messages sent in while a turn is already running can also go unanswered.

## Why it matters
A promise to report back that never gets kept trains people to stop trusting the promise, and to go check manually instead.

## Evidence
Signal: `turn_failed` (via `count`), for the case where a turn ends with no reply text. At seeding: a meaningful share of messages sent into an already-running turn got no direct reply at all. Fixed when that no-reply case stays near zero for person-started turns.

## Where the fix belongs
In what happens at the end of a turn that promised a follow-up, and in how a message sent mid-turn gets answered.

Seen: 0 times since seeding

title: It states guesses as settled fact
body:
## What goes wrong
An answer gets stated with full confidence when it was actually a guess, and the correction comes later, if at all.

## Why it matters
A confident wrong answer costs more to recover from than "I'm not sure" would have, because the listener has already acted on it.

## Evidence
No signal in the current measurement set tracks this directly. At seeding: around ten such guesses were later walked back once the real answer turned out to be different. Fixed when the rate of retracted claims drops to close to zero.

## Where the fix belongs
In how confidence gets represented when an answer hasn't actually been checked.

Seen: 0 times since seeding

title: It doesn't know its own setup
body:
## What goes wrong
Asked a basic question about how it's configured -- what it can reach, what's running where -- it gets the answer wrong.

## Why it matters
Not knowing your own setup leads to wrong assumptions downstream, and it's a question people have to ask more than once to get a trustworthy answer to.

## Evidence
No signal in the current measurement set tracks this directly. At seeding: this happened on the order of several times across a few hundred messages from people. Fixed when questions about its own setup are reliably answered without needing a correction.

## Where the fix belongs
In how its own configuration is surfaced to it, so it can check rather than guess.

Seen: 0 times since seeding

title: Standing instructions don't carry across threads
body:
## What goes wrong
An instruction meant to stand going forward only sticks in the thread it was given in; a new thread has no memory of it and the same instruction has to be repeated.

## Why it matters
Repeating the same standing instruction over and over is a sign that it isn't actually standing -- it's being re-taught each time, which wastes a person's attention on something they already said once.

## Evidence
No signal in the current measurement set tracks this directly. At seeding: one instruction had to be repeated across roughly half a dozen separate threads. Fixed when a standing instruction given once keeps applying across later threads without being repeated.

## Where the fix belongs
In how a standing instruction is saved so it's available outside the thread it was given in.

Seen: 0 times since seeding

title: Tools it needs aren't in its own runner image
body:
## What goes wrong
Partway through a turn, it reaches for a tool that turns out not to be installed in the environment it's running in.

## Why it matters
A missing tool discovered mid-turn stalls the work and forces a workaround, when the gap could have been caught and closed ahead of time.

## Evidence
Signal: `missing_tools` (via `count`). At seeding: this showed up repeatedly across transcripts as a tool simply not being found. Fixed when `missing_tools`'s total stays at zero.

## Where the fix belongs
In what the runner image ships with by default, checked against what actually gets reached for.

Seen: 0 times since seeding

title: Its token can't read CI check results
body:
## What goes wrong
The access it has to read from its code host doesn't include permission to see continuous-integration check results, so it gets an access error instead of a real pass or fail answer.

## Why it matters
Without being able to see the real check result, it has approved a change over continuous integration that was, in truth, failing -- which defeats the point of having continuous integration gate merges at all.

## Evidence
Signal: `tool_errors` (via `count`), for the access error on checks. At seeding: this access error showed up repeatedly across transcripts over the same few days. Fixed when the access error stops appearing and a real check result is read instead.

## Where the fix belongs
Only a person can widen this access; it isn't something that can be changed from inside a turn.

Seen: 0 times since seeding
